title: The Observer Effect
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart applies the 'the Queen thinks the world smells of fresh paint' thought experiment to lesson observations, arguing that leaders should stop treating performative teaching during observations as a solvable problem and instead accept it as an unavoidable feature of being watched. He identifies the underlying assumptions that drive performative behavior, teachers wanting to impress, guessing what the observer wants to see, or believing their normal practice isn't impressive enough to show, and evaluates four common leadership responses to it: asking teachers to 'just be normal' (weak, works only where trust is already high), shortening observation notice (blunt, raises anxiety and damages trust for likely no better data), increasing observation frequency (helps only if observations become developmental rather than evaluative), and simply acknowledging the effect without trying to eliminate it. Hart's preferred response is the fourth: leaders should assume a structural gap between what is seen in any single observation and typical day-to-day teaching, and use a systems-thinking 'iceberg' model where individual observations are the visible tip, requiring triangulation with other data sources over time rather than being treated as representative on their own. The piece closes by returning to the framing image, warning that leaders who fail to acknowledge the observer effect risk the same misconception the Queen was said to hold about the world always smelling of fresh paint.
points: Hart's core reframe treats the observer effect as an unremovable structural feature of observation itself, not a culture problem leaders can eventually engineer away.

He evaluates and rejects two common blunt-instrument responses (shortening notice periods, simply asking teachers to 'be normal') as ineffective or actively trust-damaging rather than accuracy-improving.

His conditional endorsement of increased observation frequency, that it only reduces the performative effect if the framing shifts from evaluative to developmental, distinguishes frequency itself from the purpose it is used for.
The systems-thinking 'iceberg' model reframes a single lesson observation as inherently partial data requiring triangulation over time, rather than a representative sample of typical teaching.

The three assumptions Hart identifies as driving performative teaching (wanting to impress, guessing what's wanted, believing normal practice isn't special enough) give leaders a diagnostic vocabulary for understanding what's actually happening inside an observed lesson.
quotes: Without asking for or expecting this, Elizabeth II would nevertheless have had an effect on people's decisions and behaviours simply by being there. And when we set up lesson observations, we can expect a similar phenomenon whether we like it or not.

The result of these assumptions is that some lesson observations are inevitably performative. Is this a problem? Not necessarily, but if leaders walk away thinking that what they saw is typical, they will have a skewed view of school life.

This is a rather blunt solution and even though it may reduce the performative element, it is highly likely to increase anxiety and affect trust. It can easily come across as seeking to catch teachers out despite espoused reasons not claiming that.
It is tempting to think that we can remove the observer effect by getting the culture right. But culture is not universal and the observer effect is human nature that extends beyond schools.
Any observation from a lesson is the tip of the iceberg. A tranche of lesson observations at any given point in time still just tells us that tip.
The world might smell of fresh paint to the Queen and unless we acknowledge the observer effect, we risk the same misconception.
